content_voiceover: This Kaplan Meier curve from Blood addresses an important clinical question, should asymptomatic relatives of thrombophilia patients be screened. The graph plots venous thrombosis free survival against age for relatives carrying different thrombophilic defects. Notice how the curves cluster into two distinct groups. Antithrombin deficiency, protein C deficiency, and protein S deficiency, the top three curves numbered one through three, show a steep decline in thrombosis free survival starting in the twenties and thirties, dropping to around thirty to forty percent by age seventy. In sharp contrast, Factor V Leiden, high Factor VIII, prothrombin G20210A, and the no-defect group, curves four through seven, stay much closer to the reference line, remaining above seventy percent thrombosis free survival even at age seventy. The log rank p value is highly significant at less than zero point zero zero one. The clinical implication is that these are not equivalent risk factors. Antithrombin, protein C, and protein S deficiencies confer a much higher lifetime thrombosis risk than Factor V Leiden or prothrombin mutations, which supports selectively screening and counseling relatives who carry the high risk deficiencies, while relatives with the more common but milder mutations may need less aggressive surveillance.
keypoints: Antithrombin, protein C, and protein S deficiency confer much higher lifetime VTE risk
Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A carriers have near-normal thrombosis free survival
Curves separate clearly by age thirty to forty
Log rank p less than 0.001 confirms the difference is significant
Supports risk-stratified screening of asymptomatic relatives
keypoint_voiceover: The natural anticoagulant deficiencies, antithrombin, protein C, and protein S, carry a much steeper lifetime thrombosis risk than Factor V Leiden or prothrombin G20210A, which should guide how aggressively you screen and counsel asymptomatic relatives.
